hood_landmark.Temple Bar: cobbled lanes centred on the famous red Temple Bar pub
hood_landmark.Ballsbridge: Aviva Stadium amid embassy-lined Victorian avenues
hood_landmark.Rathmines: the copper-domed Church of Mary Immaculate on the main street
hood_landmark.The Liberties: the Guinness Storehouse at St James's Gate
hood_landmark.Smithfield: Jameson Distillery Bow St. on the old cobbled market square

avoid.reason: Pickpocketing and anti-social behaviour around O'Connell St, the north inner city and some Luas stops at night

hood_desc: Temple Bar is Dublin's cobbled tourist and nightlife hub of pubs, live music and revelry, lively but pricey, best for partygoers and first-timers wanting to be in the thick of it.
Ballsbridge is a leafy, affluent embassy district of Georgian and Victorian homes, upscale hotels and rugby at the Aviva Stadium, suited to luxury and quieter, refined stays.
Rathmines is a popular residential and student neighborhood just south of the center, with relaxed cafes, pubs and good value, appealing to budget travelers and longer stays.
The Liberties is one of Dublin's oldest working-class quarters, home to the Guinness Storehouse and whiskey distilleries, gritty and increasingly hip for history and craft-drink fans.
Smithfield is a regenerated northside square district around the Jameson distillery with cocktail bars and a cinema, a trendy, up-and-coming base for younger travelers.

water.note: Tap water is safe and well-regulated across the city.

transit.pay: Get a TFI Leap Card — fares are far cheaper than cash singles, and the 90-minute fare (about 2 EUR) covers transfers between bus, Luas and DART. The Leap Visitor Card (1 day ~10 EUR, 3 days ~20 EUR/~US$23, 7 days ~40 EUR) gives unlimited travel and is sold at Dublin Airport and city Leap agents. Contactless bank cards are not yet accepted on city buses, Luas or DART.
transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5am-11:30pm with several 24-hour routes and Nitelink on weekend nights; Luas runs about 5:30am-12:30am.

food.name: Dublin coddle
food.desc: The city's own one-pot supper of pork sausages, rashers, onion and potato slowly stewed together. Comfort food, best with brown bread.

places.name: The Hairy Lemon
places.note: Old-school pub that has served coddle for decades; the version most Dubliners send visitors to.

places.name: The Brazen Head
places.note: Ireland's oldest pub, dating to 1198; coddle and Guinness stew alongside nightly trad music.

places.name: O'Neill's
places.note: Warren of snugs off Grafton Street with a carvery that keeps coddle on daily.

food.name: Boxty
food.desc: Potato pancake from the Irish midlands, rolled around beef, lamb or seafood. Somewhere between a crepe and a hash brown.

places.name: Gallagher's Boxty House
places.note: The city's boxty specialist; the Gaelic boxty with peppered beef is the signature order.

places.name: The Woollen Mills
places.note: Modern Irish kitchen overlooking the Liffey doing lighter, contemporary boxty plates.

places.name: Darkey Kelly's
places.note: Busy trad-music pub serving boxty and other Irish staples until late.

food.name: Seafood chowder
food.desc: Creamy soup of smoked haddock, salmon, mussels and potato, always served with buttered brown soda bread.

places.name: The Winding Stair
places.note: Bookshop-turned-restaurant on the Liffey; Irish produce cooking and a much-praised chowder.

places.name: Klaw
places.note: Tiny crab-and-oyster shack; chowder plus native oysters shucked in front of you.

places.name: The Cliff Townhouse
places.note: Elegant seafood room on the Green, strong on Irish shellfish and a refined chowder.

food.name: Irish stew and beef in Guinness
food.desc: Lamb or mutton slow-cooked with root vegetables, or beef braised in stout until it falls apart. The default Dublin pub dinner.

places.name: The Brazen Head
places.note: Widely rated for the best Irish stew in the city, in Dublin's most historic pub room.

places.name: 1837 Bar & Brasserie
places.note: Named for the year Guinness met oysters; stout-braised beef with skyline views.

places.name: The Celt
places.note: Small snug pub with live trad every night and honest stew and chowder.

food.name: Irish oysters and Dublin Bay prawns
food.desc: Carlingford and Achill oysters plus sweet langoustines from Dublin Bay. Traditionally eaten with a pint of stout, not wine.

places.name: Klaw
places.note: Standing-room seafood bar, oysters by the half dozen and lobster rolls to order.

places.name: The Seafood Cafe
places.note: Sister spot to Klaw from chef Niall Sabongi; oysters, prawns and shellfish plates.

places.name: Matt the Thresher
places.note: Long-running seafood bar near the Green with a proper oyster counter.

food.name: Full Irish breakfast
food.desc: Rashers, sausage, egg, tomato, and the two things that make it Irish: black and white pudding, with soda bread on the side.

places.name: Queen of Tarts
places.note: Cosy cafe near Dublin Castle; long queues for the Irish breakfast and homemade scones.

places.name: Bewley's Grafton Street
places.note: Grand 1927 cafe with Harry Clarke stained glass; a Dublin institution for breakfast.

places.name: The Woollen Mills
places.note: Good-quality Irish produce version, served all morning with river views.

food.name: Guinness
food.desc: Brewed at St James's Gate since 1759. A properly poured Dublin pint is settled in two stages and tastes creamier than anywhere else.

places.name: John Kavanagh (The Gravediggers)
places.note: Family-run since 1833 beside Glasnevin Cemetery; regularly voted Dublin's best pint.

places.name: Mulligan's
places.note: Unchanged 1782 pub near Trinity, famous among locals for its pour.

places.name: The Long Hall
places.note: Victorian mirrors, chandeliers and a slow, careful pint; no food, just drink.

food.name: Irish whiskey
food.desc: Triple-distilled and smoother than Scotch. Single pot still is the uniquely Irish style, made from malted and unmalted barley.

places.name: The Palace Bar
places.note: 1823 journalists' pub with its own whiskey bonding room upstairs and a huge back bar.

places.name: Teeling Whiskey Distillery
places.note: First new Dublin distillery in 125 years; tours end with a tasting flight.

places.name: Jameson Distillery Bow St
places.note: The original 1780 distillery site, now tastings and comparative whiskey classes.

landmarks: Trinity College Dublin
Ireland's oldest university, with a picturesque cobbled campus and the historic Campanile bell tower as its signature photo spot.
Book of Kells (Old Library, Trinity College)
A dazzlingly illuminated 9th-century manuscript displayed alongside the awe-inspiring barrel-vaulted Long Room library.
Dublin Castle
A former seat of British rule in Ireland, admired for its blend of medieval towers and elegant Georgian State Apartments.
Ha'penny Bridge
An elegant white cast-iron pedestrian bridge over the River Liffey, one of Dublin's most iconic and photographed structures.
Guinness Storehouse
A landmark brewery-turned-museum topped by the panoramic Gravity Bar, offering 360-degree views over the city.
St Patrick's Cathedral
Ireland's largest cathedral, a soaring Gothic structure with beautifully manicured grounds ideal for architectural photography.
Christ Church Cathedral
A medieval cathedral with a striking flying-buttress bridge to its Synod Hall, one of Dublin's oldest surviving buildings.
Temple Bar
Dublin's colorful cultural quarter, famous for its cobbled lanes and the iconic red-fronted Temple Bar pub.
Phoenix Park
One of Europe's largest enclosed city parks, known for free-roaming deer and expansive green vistas near the city center.
Spire of Dublin
A slender 120m stainless-steel monument on O'Connell Street that gleams and catches light, forming a modern focal point of the city skyline.

train.note: The cross-border Enterprise runs roughly hourly from Dublin Connolly to Belfast Grand Central. No passport control on the land border (Common Travel Area), but non-Irish/UK citizens should carry their documents.

bus.note: Frequent cross-border coaches: Expressway X1/X2 leave from Busáras and Dublin Airport; Aircoach runs from the city centre and airport. Ireland has no other land borders, so all other international travel is by ferry or air.

ferry.note: All sailings leave from Dublin Port, about 3 km from the centre. Holyhead takes ~3h15 with onward trains to London; Cherbourg is an overnight crossing of ~18h, several times a week. Bring your passport for France.

half.name: Glendalough & Wicklow Mountains
half.blurb: A serene glacial valley with monastic ruins and lakes cradled by wild green mountains.

half.name: Howth
half.blurb: A charming fishing village with cliff walks, fresh seafood, and sweeping views over Dublin Bay.

half.name: Kilkenny
half.blurb: A medieval city crowned by a grand castle, cobbled lanes, and a lively craft scene.

half.name: Boyne Valley & Newgrange
half.blurb: Ancient passage tombs older than the pyramids scattered across lush, history-soaked countryside.

half.name: Malahide Castle
half.blurb: A storybook medieval castle set in expansive gardens beside a pretty seaside town.

full.name: Belfast
full.blurb: Northern Ireland's vibrant capital, rich with maritime history, murals, and Titanic heritage.
